title: Prototype Focus-Group Report and Evidence Audit
paragraphs: Appendix G Prototype Focus-Group Report and Evidence Audit This appendix incorporates the merged FGD report. Its narrative-level ndings inform Sections 6.7 and 5.9; the underlying participant records remain unveried; a 160-segment machine transcript is included, but speaker attribution and human verication are pending. G.1 Purpose and Evidentiary Scope This report integrates two narrative accounts of a focus-group discussion (FGD) involving university students and a walkthrough of LOKLOK, a proposed social media radio application. Its purpose is to clarify the audience needs and design questions suggested by those accounts: the relationship between listening and creating, the appeal and constraints of collaborative broadcasting, expectations around institutional access, and the usability of a wireframe interface. It does not establish the platform's originality, market success, or eects on student behaviour. The material comprises the earlier narrative (Account A) and the expanded narrative supplied as FGD2.tex (Account B), together with their PDFs. Account A is retained in the source archive, while this document is the merged report. The two 268

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT 269 narratives repeat the same four domains, lexical counts, and frame references. They are therefore treated as overlapping accounts of one reported session, not two focus groups, independent corroboration, or separate participant samples. A 160-segment machine transcript of the session audio is included. The audiovisual recordings, speaker attribution, and participant roster remain unavailable; the transcript is used for semantic embedding, not for audited quotation. A subsequently supplied le, fgd_analysis_parts.json, contains seven model-generated summaries. It is designated Supplement C, not another focus group or an independent corroborating source. The proposed revised LaTeX accompanying that export is treated as a set of candidate claims to review, not as evidence that the primary materials have been recovered. Section G.4 records the adjudication. Throughout, reported account means a statement present in either supplied narrative; interpretation means an analytical reading of that account; and verication requirement identies the evidence needed to assess it. None of these labels turns a paraphrase into a participant quotation. Focus groups derive their distinctive value from interaction among participants, including exchanges, disagreements, and responses to one another, rather than simply collecting several individual opinions at once (Kitzinger, 1995). In this case, the distinction between a moderator-led product demonstration and participant-led discussion is especially important. Both accounts report extensive moderator explanation, but the balance of contributions cannot be established without speakerlabelled records. Statements explaining how LOKLOK is intended to work are therefore not treated as evidence that participants endorsed those features.

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT 270 G.2 Study Context and Reporting Completeness Both accounts describe a university conference-room session conducted in colloquial Egyptian Arabic, an English translation, and smartphone interaction with application wireframes. Account B explicitly situates the proposed campus restriction in the Ahram Canadian University (ACU) context. This claries the reported institutional setting without establishing each participant's aliation, the exact venue, recruitment procedure, or ethics review. Account A gives an approximate duration of 28 minutes; Account B reports 1,675.33 seconds (27 minutes 55.33 seconds). These descriptions are compatible as rounded and more precise reported durations. The latter is not newly measured metadata, however, and it does not resolve the visual reference at 30 minutes 30 seconds. Section G.9 reconciles the arithmetic and records the remaining source discrepancy. Additional recording details from Account B are retained in Section G.8. Table G.1 identies the principal information needed for a source-based report. COREQ oers reporting prompts for interviews and focus groups, while APA's qualitative reporting standards emphasise the transparent presentation of research design, researcher involvement, analysis, and evidence (Levitt et al., 2018; Tong et al., 2007). These sources guide the audit; citing them does not establish checklist compliance, ethical approval, or study quality.

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT 271 Table G.1: Reporting Status and Required Source Documentation Domain Available account Documentation required Session and setting University conference room; ACU context in Account B; two compatible reported durations. Date, exact venue, session identity, source-le duration, and common timestamp origin. Participants and recruitment University students; no auditable roster or sample size supplied. Number invited and attending, eligibility, recruitment route, relevant sample characteristics, and nonparticipation where recorded. Researcher relationship Moderator explains the prototype; role and prior relationships are unspecied. Moderator identity and role, training, institutional relationships, and involvement in product design. Procedure and prototype Wireframe walkthrough and smartphone interaction described. Topic guide, task instructions, prototype version, features actually available, and sequence of demonstration and discussion. Recording and language Arabic speech, translation, visual frames, and technical audio gures reported. Original les, extraction settings, speaker-labelled transcript, translation decisions, and source-linked observation log. Analysis Four domains, lexical counts, and interpretive statements supplied. Coding records, analysts' roles, dated decisions, source extracts, alternative readings, and count specications. Ethics and data stewardship Approval, consent, condentiality, and reuse arrangements not documented in the supplied les. Applicable review decision, participant information and permissions, storage/access arrangements, and disclosure or reuse restrictions. Unknown characteristics must remain unknown: neither a particular age cohort nor demographic diversity can be inferred from the label university students. No survey sample size elsewhere in the thesis is assigned to this FGD. Nor can sampling adequacy or saturation be asserted from the length of the account. The information-power approach relates qualitative sample adequacy to the study aim, sample specicity, theoretical framing, dialogue, and analysis strategy rather than to a universal numerical threshold (Malterud et al., 2016). Developed for individual

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT 272 interview studies, that approach does not prescribe the number or composition of focus groups. Those considerations cannot yet be assessed here. G.3 Analytical Approach and Source Verication G.3.1 A Provisional, Framework-Informed Reading The revision retains the four shared domains as provisional organising categories and integrates Account B's proposed links to the thesis framework. The domains were not newly generated through inductive coding of a transcript. Thematic analysis involves interpreting patterned meaning, and its theoretical and procedural choices should be explicit (Braun & Clarke, 2006). Here, the immediate aim is narrower: to distinguish reported experiences, moderator explanations, analytical interpretations, and proposed design responses without overstating their evidentiary status. If primary records become available, a framework-informed analysis would be a suitable option to consider. A matrix can link cases or interaction episodes to categories while retaining contextual summaries and source references (Gale et al., 2013). The present codebook is a starting point for that work, not proof that it has been performed. New categories, contradictory cases, and revisions to the initial four domains must remain possible. The researcher should identify the chosen analytical tradition rather than combine incompatible quality criteria: intercoder agreement is not a universal requirement of reexive thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2021). No agreement statistic or independent coding is claimed here.

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT 273 G.3.2 Language, Translation, and Quotations Translation is an interpretive part of qualitative research, not a neutral replacement of words. Decisions about idiom and expression can alter meaning (van Nes et al., 2010). For this study, a proposed verication record should retain the Egyptian Arabic extract alongside the English translation, with a speaker code, source timestamp, and a note explaining consequential translation choices. A bilingual review should be documented if undertaken, not assumed. Ambiguity, disagreement, or hesitation should not be removed merely to produce more uent academic prose. Because no primary transcript or recording was supplied, this report provides no purported verbatim participant quotations. Supplement C contains text labelled as original Arabic and translations, but those labels do not establish transcription delity or speaker identity. The underlying strings are retained in the controlled review record, not promoted into participant testimony. Expressions used as interface names or analytical labels, such as Boost and Podcast Paradox, are not presented as quotations from identied participants. Before an extract is published as evidence, its wording, translation, attribution, and permitted use must be checked against the original record. An unintelligible segment should remain marked as uncertain rather than reconstructed from expectations. G.3.3 Proposed Verication Sequence The following sequence is a prospective procedure for this material, not a retrospective account of completed analysis: 1. Establish a le inventory and preserve the original recording, transcript, pro-

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT 274 totype version, and permissions records. Assign stable le identiers and document any edited or translated derivatives. 2. Reconcile the recording duration and timestamp origin. Link each extract and observation to the same source version; document osets where necessary. 3. Identify participant and moderator turns using pseudonymous codes. Retain the surrounding exchange so that prompted agreement is distinguishable from an independently introduced concern. 4. Review the Arabic and English records together. Record uncertain speech, translation choices, overlapping speech, and observable actions separately. 5. Apply and revise the provisional codebook. Maintain source-linked analytical memos, including divergent experiences and explanations that do not support the anticipated design benet. 6. Reassess every thematic claim and any descriptive count against those records. Report only the procedures actually completed and retain an audit trail of changes. G.4 Review of the Supplemental Analysis Export Supplement C is a JSON array of seven text strings, each containing generated questions, proposed answers, themes, or quality cautions. It contains neither a structured primary transcript with attributable turns nor a collection of 20 visual frames. No recording, frame images, source-to-output alignment, prompt, execution

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT 275 log, or independently reviewed translation accompanies it. The researcher identies the export as output from an instruction-tuned 7B model; the le itself does not establish the exact model version, quantisation, input coverage, or generation settings. The admissible contribution is an additional set of review leads and a record of limitations in the generated analysis. It does not change the primary-evidence status reported in Section G.1. References to unveried speakers occur in the output, but no inspected transcript supports the stronger claim that every original segment carries that label. Nor may an unattributed sentence be reassigned to the moderator or the group merely because that role seems plausible. G.4.1 Internal Consistency and Translation Checks Part numbers below are one-based positions in the supplied JSON array, not participant identiers or independently timed recording segments. In Part 2, an Arabic expression referring to a room is paired with an English rendering that locates the microphone in a car. Part 1 renders a colloquial vehicle-listening expression as listening in the Arabic language. These are translation inconsistencies within the export; identifying them does not verify that either extract was actually spoken. Named-person renderings also require checking against the recording rather than being accepted from the English gloss alone. Translation choices should preserve source meaning and uncertainty rather than create a more uent but altered account (van Nes et al., 2010). Some purported extracts contain Chinese or Cyrillic material mixed with Arabic, while several timestamps are incomplete, malformed, or placeholders. Part 5

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT 276 includes a placeholder rather than an actual time interval. Parts 1 and 4 end with apparently unnished text. These observations warrant review of the original inputs and generation logs; they do not establish why the artefacts occurred. No missing words, speakers, or time boundaries are reconstructed to make the export appear complete. Table G.2: Adjudication of the Supplemental Export and Proposed Revision Candidate addition Decision Reason and permitted use A supplemental sevenpart analysis export is available Accepted as an artefact Its existence and text can be inspected; it is not primary participant data or another sample. Attention to speaker uncertainty, translation, and ambiguous vocalisations Retained as a safeguard These are appropriate review requirements, not completed source verication or validated non-speech labels. Variation in willingness to hear long podcasts; registration-error questions Retained as review questions Parts 2 and 3 suggest topics to investigate; no veried preference, task failure, or new theme frequency is inferred. Primary transcript and 20-frame visual log recovered and triangulated Not established Those materials are not supplied. Generated descriptions cannot certify their recovery, completeness, or alignment. Verbatim quotations, precise intervals, and moderator/participant roles Withheld as evidence The original wording, speaker, and interval remain unchecked; some text and timestamps are internally inconsistent. Consensus, retention gains, lower anxiety, safety, or intuitive usability Not established The export supplies neither a veried interaction record nor outcome measures supporting these claims. A validated Podcast Paradox, automatic resolution through cohosting, or EST-P3 validation through ID/PIN Not accepted as ndings An analytic label is not a validated construct; a design description is not a causal test or a psychometric assessment.

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT 277 G.4.2 What Changes in the Interpretation The four provisional domains remain in place. Supplement C suggests checking whether preferred programme length varies and whether registration instructions or error feedback are understood. These are follow-up questions within FGD-T1 and FGD-T4, not newly established participant experiences. Its account of unrestricted access also conicts with the campus-only descriptions in Accounts A and B; this is retained as an unresolved discrepancy, not evidence that the participants debated or agreed on an open-access policy. Repeated vocalisation-like strings in Parts 57 are treated as unresolved transcript artefacts. They are not coded as silence, non-participation, hesitation, a technical failure, or active wireframe use without checking the recording and aligned visual evidence. Sparse or uninterpretable output cannot establish that no substantive speech occurred. Likewise, generated statements that everyone agreed do not establish consensus when the original interaction and speakers are unavailable. The proposed bilingual quotations are consequently not inserted as empirical extracts. A review record retains the candidate wording, its JSON part locator, the disputed rendering, and the decision needed before use. No synthetic quote becomes a participant record, calibration weight, factual answer key, or prompt instruction to reproduce a favourable outcome. The export may inform quality checks and later source review, but does not independently conrm the existing themes or validate either proposed simulation engine.

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT 278 G.5 Provisional Thematic Interpretation The four domains below synthesise the two supplied narratives, not newly veried transcripts. Supplement C has been reviewed for candidate additions but is not treated as independent corroboration. Each separates the reported account from its possible meaning and the limits of that interpretation. External methodological citations explain how the material is handled; they do not authenticate the local observations. G.5.1 FGD-T1: Contextual Listening and Selective Publication Reported account. Both accounts describe listening during travel and at home, interest in radio storytelling, and a reference to older radio serials. They also recount an individual who owns a microphone and records privately but does not publish those recordings. Account B explicitly attributes this practice to self-training and preparation and says that recordings are discarded. This reported explanation is retained, but speaker identity, verbatim wording, and interactional context remain unveried in the machine transcript. Interpretation. The account suggests a useful distinction between listening, practising, and publishing. Possessing recording equipment or enjoying audio does not necessarily imply a wish to broadcast publicly. The draft calls this tension the Podcast Paradox; here, that expression is retained only as a provisional analytical label, not a validated construct or a demonstrated characteristic of the wider student population. Alternative readings and implications. Unpublished recordings could

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT 279 reect deliberate private practice, privacy preferences, limited time, self-imposed production standards, or a lack of interest in an audience. The reported self-training explanation deserves priority over an imposed anxiety interpretation, although its meaning and context still require source checking. Other explanations should be explored, not attributed to that individual without evidence. A defensible design question is therefore whether students want dierent routes from listening to private practice, collaborative creation, and public sharing. Non-public participation should not automatically be framed as failure or a decit. G.5.2 FGD-T2: Collaborative Broadcasting and Choice Reported account. The moderator reportedly described a broadcasting mechanic requiring a peer invitation or co-host. The narrative characterises the reaction as favourable, but provides no attributable extracts, contrary responses, or evidence of subsequent use. Account B also develops an analogy with traditional radio call-ins: inviting a peer to co-host is presented as a way to make the broadcast a shared conversation. This is the account's design rationale, not evidence that a caller's role and a co-host's role are equivalent. The rule is treated as part of the walkthrough description, not as a veried feature of a deployed application. Interpretation. Co-hosting is a candidate means of making an audio exchange feel conversational rather than like an individual performance. This is a plausible reading of the accounts, not a measured reduction in anxiety, eort, or cognitive demand. Source-based analysis should ask who introduced this idea and how others responded, preserving the interaction rather than counting armative words alone (Kitzinger, 1995).

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT 280 Alternative readings and implications. Mandatory co-hosting might also restrict participation when a peer is unavailable, when a student prefers independent expression, or when social exposure is unwelcome. These are design questions proposed in this review, not diculties demonstrated in the session. Optional co-hosting, private rehearsal, and alternative contribution routes should be compared with the mandatory model before claiming that one arrangement lowers barriers for everyone. G.5.3 FGD-T3: Institutional Eligibility, Trust, and Privacy Reported account. Both accounts describe a university-ID and PIN entry process, explained through an ATM analogy, and a platform initially limited to university students, with Account B naming the ACU context. The narratives attribute benets involving trust and community to this arrangement, but do not supply participantlevel evidence of those judgements or an assessment of the authentication system. Interpretation. Institutional eligibility, perceived trust, condentiality, and technical security are separate questions. The described entry rule alone establishes none of the latter three. In particular, restricting membership does not demonstrate the absence of harassment, prove the validity of research responses, or show that students feel comfortable speaking under an institutional identity. Alternative readings and implications. A bounded community could be welcoming for some students and expose others to unwanted visibility. The next evaluation should ask what identity information is displayed, who can access recordings, how complaints are handled, and whether eligible students can obtain or recover access. Preferences for named and pseudonymous participation should

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT 281 be explored rather than presumed. These are proposed evaluation topics; neither preference nor a security outcome was measured in the material available here. G.5.4 FGD-T4: Interface Cues, Invitations, and Idle Content Reported account. The narrative describes proles, avatars, names, timestamps, a text-based Boost invitation, and music or advertising when no broadcast is active. It also reports smartphone interaction during the walkthrough. The available documents do not establish which functions were interactive, which were static representations, or which were explained only by the moderator. Interpretation. These descriptions identify candidate interface functions: communicating who is present, inviting an audience, and explaining what happens when no conversation is available. They do not demonstrate successful navigation, low cognitive load, sustained engagement, or an intuitive interface. Such conclusions would require task-linked evidence and the participants' own accounts, not merely a statement that screens were tapped or swiped. Alternative readings and implications. Future evaluation should consider whether invitations are understandable, whether idle-state content is clearly identied, and whether users can control unwanted playback. Relevant accessibility checks can draw on WCAG 2.2, including applicable text alternatives, contrast, navigation, and media-control criteria (World Wide Web Consortium, 2024). This is a proposal for evaluation, not a nding of accessibility or a claim of conformance by the prototype. Applicable criteria must be selected for the actual interface and media format.

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT 282 G.6 Working Codebook and Relationships Table G.3 provides operational boundaries for a future review of the primary records. Codes should be assigned to source-linked segments, not to entire people. A segment may have more than one relevant code; a moderator's feature description must remain distinguishable from a participant's experience, question, or evaluation. These are proposed coding conventions for this report, not a completed coding result. Table G.3: Provisional Codebook for Source-Based Review Domain Include when supported by the source Boundary and evidence requirement FGD-T1: Listening and publication Listening contexts; private practice; expressed reasons for publishing or not publishing. Exclude assumptions that listening implies a wish to broadcast. Retain the speaker's explanation and surrounding exchange. FGD-T2: Collaboration and choice Co-host descriptions; preferences for shared or independent creation; expressed participation constraints. Separate moderator proposals from participant responses. Do not code agreement as reduced anxiety unless that meaning is expressed. FGD-T3: Eligibility and trust Access rules; stated expectations or concerns about identity, privacy, trust, and inclusion. Do not infer safety from membership restrictions. Record whether a claim concerns a preference, a concern, or an experienced event. FGD-T4: Interface and idle content Task-linked navigation, interpretations of interface cues, invitations, and responses to inactiveroom content. Separate displayed, demonstrated, and proposed functions. Link actions to the task, timestamp, and accompanying explanation. The proposed connections in Table G.4 organise questions for further investigation. They are not causal eects estimated from this FGD. Neither the order of the walkthrough nor co-occurrence in a narrative establishes that one theme produces another.

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT 283 Table G.4: Candidate Relationships and Competing Interpretations Connection Question suggested by the accounts Competing interpretation to examine FGD-T1 and FGD-T2 Does co-hosting oer a desirable route from private practice to sharing? Some students may prefer privacy or independent production regardless of collaboration. FGD-T2 and FGD-T3 Does restricted membership affect willingness to invite peers or speak publicly? Recognisable institutional identities may increase unwanted visibility rather than comfort. FGD-T2 and FGD-T4 Do invitations and presence cues help students coordinate a shared broadcast? A feature may be visible but misunderstood, inaccessible, or unwanted. FGD-T1 and FGD-T4 Do interface and idle-state choices support dierent listening contexts? Automatic music, advertising, or prompts to contribute may conict with a listener's preferences. G.6.1 Relationship to Epistemic Systems Theory Account B links the domains to Epistemic Systems Theory (EST), the framework proposed by the thesis author. This theoretical reading is retained as a sensitising interpretation: it identies questions to investigate, not propositions conrmed by the FGD. It follows the narrative synthesis rather than replacing source-based analysis. A framework matrix can make such interpretive connections traceable while keeping the original evidence and alternative readings visible (Gale et al., 2013). In particular, Account B's alignment of institutional exclusivity with EST-P3 needs qualication. In the thesis, EST-P3 concerns the psychometric accountability of consequential metrics. This FGD account supplies neither a measurement model nor reliability or validity evidence for such a metric. Institutional access may be discussed as governance context, but cannot stand in for psychometric validation. Likewise, no network-diversity or misinformation-diusion observations are supplied

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT 284 Table G.5: Bounded Connections Between the FGD Domains and EST Domain and link Interpretive contribution Boundary of inference FGD-T1; EST-P4 Distinguishes opportunities to practise, participate, and publish. No observed source appraisal, correction, or improvement in evidence-based production. FGD-T2; EST-P1 Identies co-hosting rules as a proposed inuence on participation. No comparison establishes that architecture primarily determines behaviour or quality. FGD-T3; governance context Identies identity, access, and privacy questions relevant to participation. An ID/PIN rule is not a psychometric instrument and does not itself test EST-P3. FGD-T4; EST-P1 and EST-P4 Identies interface cues and invitations as possible supports for interaction. Screen activity does not demonstrate epistemic improvement or establish an eect of those cues. to assess EST-P2. The integrated interpretation is therefore about participation choices within a proposed design, not demonstrated epistemic gains. Private practice may be an intended activity rather than failed publication; collaboration may be welcome without being compulsory; and institutional membership may be valued without implying comfort with identiable speech. These alternatives connect the four domains without forcing all accounts into a single product success narrative. Any later linkage to survey ndings must distinguish qualitative meanings from numerical associations and establish the provenance of each dataset before claiming convergence. G.7 Lexical Counts: Audit and Proposed Reanalysis Both accounts assign the same frequencies to six grouped English terms, but no transcript, search dictionary, tokenisation rule, or speaker-specic denominator accompanies them. Table G.6 preserves those gures for traceability only. Repetition

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT 285 across the accounts is not replication, and the gures are not added together. They are not independently reproduced results and are excluded from the substantive conclusions of this report. The six categories must not be summed into a corpus size: overlap, eligibility, and unit of counting are unspecied. Table G.6: Unveried Frequencies Repeated in Both Accounts Draft category Reported count Radio / Audio 24 University / Students 18 Alone / Solo 9 Together / Invite 12 Wireframe / Interface 15 Record / Microphone 7 Note. These numbers describe what both accounts report, not what an independently inspected transcript contains. They do not establish the relative importance of themes or participant endorsement. In summative qualitative content analysis, counts are followed by contextual interpretation; they do not replace it (Hsieh & Shannon, 2005). For this FGD, a term could appear in a moderator explanation, a participant's objection, or an unrelated example. Its repetition alone cannot establish interest, trust, or a psychological barrier. Counts from an English translation must also be identied as counts of that translation, not as frequencies in the original Arabic speech. If lexical analysis is retained, the researcher should rst specify the corpus version, eligible speaker turns, treatment of llers, word boundaries, case and inection handling, category dictionary, and overlapping matches. One proposed descriptive measure is the frequency per 1,000 eligible words within each speaker role: fkr = 1000 nkr Nr , Nr > 0, (G.1)

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT 286 where k denotes a predened term category, r denotes the speaker role (moderator or participants), nkr is its number of eligible word-token matches, and Nr is the total number of eligible word tokens for that role. Each word token should count at most once within a given category; any cross-category overlap should be disclosed. In plain language: count how often the specied words appear, divide by the total words spoken by that role, and scale the result to 1,000 words. Keeping moderator and participant speech separate prevents a long product explanation from being mistaken for audience interest. This measure remains descriptive; it does not show whether the words express agreement or concern. A second optional measure is participant mention coverage: ck = 1 n n X i=1 1(nki > 0), n > 0, (G.2) where n is the documented number of eligible participants with analysable records, nki is the number of matches for category k in participant i's speech, and 1(nki > 0) equals one if that participant mentions the category at least once and zero otherwise. Exclusions from the denominator must be reported. In plain language: this is the proportion of eligible participants who mention a category at least once. It prevents one frequent speaker from being counted as several people, but it does not measure endorsement or importance. A zero can reect limited opportunity to speak, and cannot be read as indierence. Neither measure is calculated here because a speaker-attributed transcript and the participant denominator are unavailable. These equations are proposed reporting denitions for a future reanalysis, not estimates of population opinion or tests of causality.

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT 287 G.8 Reported Recording Characteristics Account B supplies technical gures that were absent from Account A. They are retained in Table G.7 so that the eventual source-le check has explicit targets. Their precision does not establish their accuracy: neither the audio nor the technical notes referred to in Account B were provided. These gures describe a purported recording or its processing, not participant demographics or qualitative ndings. Table G.7: Recording Characteristics Reported in Account B Characteristic Reported value Required check or interpretation Duration 1,675.33 s Check the source le and any trimming; reconcile the time origin with the visual log. Sample rate 16,000 Hz Check le metadata and whether resampling occurred. This is not a participant count. Audio channels One (mono) Check whether this is the original or a converted le; a single channel does not imply a single speaker. Mean RMS 0.13958 Establish amplitude scale, frame length, aggregation, and preprocessing before reproducing the value. Estimated speech segments 160 Establish segmentation method, settings, and manual checks. Segments are not necessarily turns, people, or meaningful exchanges. For clarity, the root-mean-square (RMS) amplitude of a block of N waveform samples xj is RMS(x) = v u u t 1 N N X j=1 x2 j, N > 0. (G.3) Here, N counts audio samples, not participants. In plain language: square the recorded sample values, take their average, and take the square root. The result

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT 288 summarises signal amplitude on the recording's numerical scale, not the meaning or quality of the discussion. Audio documentation illustrates frame-based RMS calculation and the importance of frame and padding settings (librosa, n.d.). An average of frame-level RMS values is not generally the same as one RMS computed across the whole recording. Consequently, Account B's mean RMS cannot be reproduced from the number alone; the equation claries the concept without asserting the original calculation method. The cited software is an explanatory reference, not a claim that it was used for this recording. Neither the RMS gure nor the estimated 160 segments establishes that the session was highly interactive. Before interpreting participation, a source-based review should distinguish moderator and participant turns, identify who responds to whom, and retain interruptions, disagreement, and changes of position. It should also check whether apparent agreement followed a leading description or reected an independently stated preference. These interactional questions are more relevant to focus-group interpretation than treating automatically or manually segmented audio as a measure of engagement (Kitzinger, 1995). G.9 Observational Evidence and Timing Audit Both accounts describe the same visual frames but do not supply the images, recording, or source log. Their claims of successful triangulation therefore cannot be independently assessed. Table G.8 identies a specic inconsistency that must be resolved before audiovisual evidence is used to support the thematic interpretation. These conversions are arithmetic checks of the reported values, not veri-

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT 289 Table G.8: Reconciliation of Reported Durations and Visual Timestamps Reported item Converted time Audit implication Account A: approximate duration 28:00 (1,680 s) Rounded description; 4.67 s longer than Account B's reported duration. Account B: reported duration 27:55.33 (1,675.33 s) Compatible with approximately 28 minutes; not independently measured here. Frame 12 in both accounts 20:59 (1,259 s) Within either reported duration if the time origin is shared. Frame 17 in both accounts 30:30 (1,830 s) Exceeds Account B's duration by 154.67 s; not resolved by rounding. cation of the frames. The discrepancy could involve an approximate duration, an oset, an edited recording, or an erroneous timestamp; the available material does not establish which. No replacement session duration is inferred. The proposed revision's claim that ambiguous audio aligns precisely with Frames 10, 12, and 17 is not accepted: no such frames or alignment log were supplied, and the stated Frame 17 timestamp still exceeds the reported duration by 154.67 seconds. Neither a list of selected frame numbers nor generated commentary constitutes a continuous visual record. Account B additionally describes natural light, large windows, and a semi-circular seating arrangement. These details are retained as reported context, not evidence that participants felt relaxed, included, or willing to disagree. If veried, the room arrangement can help explain sightlines and interaction opportunities; participants' comfort requires their own accounts rather than an inference from furniture or lighting. The accounts also mention interface elements in Frames 6, 7, and 9 and question overlays in Frames 17 and 19. Even if those descriptions are subsequently

APPENDIX G. FOCUS-GROUP EVIDENCE AUDIT 290 conrmed, an overlaid prompt is not a participant utterance. An image showing a phone likewise does not establish a completed task or a participant's mental state. A source-linked observation record should distinguish visible action, audible speech, analyst interpretation, and uncertainty. The label Active UX Interaction should therefore not be assigned to all prolonged vocalisations or speech gaps. Where the recording supports it, a narrower description such as screen interaction observed can record tapping or swiping without inferring comprehension, satisfaction, or cognitive immersion. Speech and device activity may overlap; absence of speech should not automatically be classied as disengagement, consent, or a usability problem. These are proposed coding boundaries, not observations newly made from the unveried machine transcript. G.10 Reexivity, Ethics, and Inclusive Interpretation Researcher position and prior commitments can shape both the research encounter and its interpretation (Berger, 2015). The accounts' product-oriented language and emphasis on favourable responses warrant particular reexive attention. The moderator's relationship to the students and the product should be documented. Enthusiasm, politeness, prompted agreement, and substantive endorsement should be considered as alternative readings, not presumed equivalent. Any institutional power relationship is a question to investigate, not a fact established by the current les. The revised report does not treat students as a homogeneous generation or assume shared levels of condence, digital access, language prociency, or willingness to appear publicly. Future recruitment and facilitation should consider whose

Listening without broadcasting, using an alternative mode of expression, or choosing not to answer must not be interpreted as lesser competence.
